title: The White House is making arcade games racist
summary: Trump’s racist new “Build the Wall” game. | Image: The White House The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed "arcade" games, some of which are racist - and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be…
whatHappening: The White House has released a series of arcade-style games with policy themes, some of which contain racist content. The games appear to reference border wall construction and other Trump administration initiatives, potentially infringing on copyrighted material from existing arcade titles.
whoInvolved: The White House communications team, under the Trump administration (Donald Trump is the 47th president of the United States), created and released these games. The games reference border policy that has been central to Trump's political platform.
whyMatters: The release raises concerns about racist content being promoted through official White House channels and platforms. It also highlights potential intellectual property violations and questions about the appropriateness of using arcade game formats—typically associated with entertainment—to promote divisive policy positions. The incident reflects broader tensions around immigration rhetoric and how government entities use digital media.
articleBody:
The White House has launched an unexpected foray into video game development, releasing a collection of arcade-style games that blend policy messaging with retro gaming aesthetics. According to The Verge, some of these games contain racist elements and appear to be modeled after classic arcade titles, raising concerns about both content and copyright compliance.

The games appear to draw inspiration from the Mexico–United States border wall project, which has been a cornerstone of Trump administration policy. A border wall has been under construction along portions of the U.S.-Mexico border as part of efforts to reduce illegal immigration. The arcade games translate this policy initiative into interactive form, though the execution has drawn criticism for incorporating offensive content.

Beyond the racial concerns, the games present potential legal complications. By modeling themselves on existing arcade games without apparent licensing agreements, the White House games may infringe on copyrights held by the original creators and rights holders. This raises questions about whether government agencies should be creating derivative works based on commercial intellectual property, particularly when doing so for political messaging.

The release underscores an unusual approach to political communication—using entertainment media traditionally designed for amusement to promote divisive policy positions. While political campaigns and administrations have long employed digital media, the specific format and content of these games represent a departure from conventional government messaging strategies.

The incident also highlights ongoing debates surrounding immigration rhetoric and the visual and cultural language used to frame border policy. The decision to embed such messaging into game form, particularly games containing racist content, raises broader questions about how government resources are deployed and what message such releases send about official priorities and values.

title: GoPro says it’s still committed ‘to your collective stoke’
summary: GoPro CEO Nick Woodman said in a letter to customers that making cameras is still his company's "core DNA," after a proposed $285 million acquisition by Starman was announced earlier this week. He claims the merger puts GoPro in a better position to continue developing its…
whatHappening: GoPro CEO Nick Woodman has reassured customers that the company remains committed to camera manufacturing as its core business, following the announcement of a proposed $285 million acquisition by Starman earlier this week. Woodman's letter emphasizes that the merger will actually strengthen GoPro's ability to develop innovative cameras and products.
whoInvolved: GoPro, Inc. is an American technology company founded by Nick Woodman in 2002 that manufactures action cameras and video-editing software for adventure sports and outdoor activities. The company went public on the Nasdaq in 2014 under ticker $GPRO and is based in San Mateo, California. Starman, the acquiring company, is pursuing the $285 million deal.
whyMatters: The acquisition raised concerns among GoPro's customer base about whether the company would abandon its foundational business of making cameras. Woodman's letter directly addresses these worries by reaffirming the company's strategic focus, signaling that the merger is intended to provide resources and partnership benefits rather than a fundamental pivot away from hardware. This messaging matters for maintaining customer confidence and clarifying the deal's purpose to stakeholders.
articleBody:
GoPro's founder and CEO Nick Woodman has moved to calm concerns about the company's future following news of Starman's proposed $285 million acquisition. In a letter to customers, Woodman stressed that making cameras remains central to GoPro's identity and business strategy, pushing back against any perception that the merger signals a departure from the company's core mission.

The acquisition announcement earlier this week prompted immediate questions about GoPro's direction, given that the company has built its reputation over two decades on manufacturing rugged action cameras for extreme sports, travel, and outdoor enthusiasts. Founded in 2002 by Woodman himself, GoPro went public on the Nasdaq in 2014 and has remained focused on camera hardware as its primary product offering, while developing complementary mobile apps and video-editing software.

Woodman's letter frames the Starman deal as an opportunity rather than a threat to this core business. According to The Verge, he characterized the merger as positioning GoPro to continue advancing camera technology and delivering what he calls the company's commitment "to your collective stoke." The language reflects GoPro's brand identity, which centers on capturing and celebrating adventure and excitement.

The timing of Woodman's direct communication to customers underscores the sensitivity around acquisitions in the tech hardware space, where changes in ownership sometimes lead to product line consolidations or strategic refocusing. By publicly reaffirming that camera manufacturing remains GoPro's "core DNA," Woodman is attempting to preempt speculation and maintain the trust of both longtime customers and potential new buyers who rely on the brand's historical commitment to action camera innovation.

The $285 million valuation and merger structure suggest this is a significant transaction for GoPro, though specifics about how Starman's involvement will materially benefit the company's product development roadmap have not yet been detailed. Woodman's reassurance that the company will continue focusing on cameras serves as a first step in explaining the strategic rationale to stakeholders who may be concerned about the acquisition's implications.

title: Audacity 4 is a complete revamp of the ‘world’s most popular’ audio editor
summary: Audacity 4 has been in the works for some time, and had its own mini controversy last year when an unfortunate redesigned logo started making the rounds. The final version of the new icon isn't nearly as bad as the early rendition that was circulating last October. But more…
whatHappening: Audacity 4, a complete overhaul of the free and open-source audio editor, has officially launched after an extended development cycle. The new version includes a redesigned logo that addresses the controversial early iterations that circulated last year.
whoInvolved: Audacity is the free and open-source digital audio editor available across Windows, macOS, Linux, and other Unix-like operating systems. The project has a large user base, with The Verge describing it as the 'world's most popular' audio editor.
whyMatters: Audacity 4 represents a significant refresh of a tool relied upon by millions of users globally, from casual podcasters to professional audio engineers. The new version's design and functionality changes signal the project's continued evolution to remain competitive and user-friendly in an increasingly crowded audio software landscape.
articleBody:
Audacity 4 has officially arrived, marking a comprehensive redesign of the free and open-source audio editing software that serves millions of users worldwide. According to The Verge, the new version represents the culmination of work that has been in development for some time, bringing updated visuals, interface improvements, and enhanced functionality to what many consider the most accessible entry point into digital audio editing.

The development process has not been without its share of public discussion. Last October, an early redesigned logo that was circulating online generated considerable pushback from the community, sparking a minor controversy around the project's aesthetic direction. However, the final icon that ships with Audacity 4 represents a more measured approach that addresses earlier concerns without alienating the user base.

Audacity itself has been a staple of audio production for years, available across Windows, macOS, Linux, and other Unix-like operating systems. As free and open-source software, it has democratized audio editing for hobbyists, students, podcasters, and professionals who might otherwise be priced out of commercial alternatives. The release of version 4 signals the maintainers' commitment to keeping the platform modern and relevant.

The complete revamp suggests more than just cosmetic changes. While specific feature additions remain partially obscured in the available summary, a full version bump from 3 to 4 typically indicates substantial architectural improvements, UI refinements, and possibly new capabilities aimed at expanding the software's appeal and functionality. Such updates are critical for retaining users who might otherwise migrate to competing tools.

For the broader audio editing community, Audacity 4's release reinforces the viability of open-source alternatives to proprietary software. The project's ability to undergo a complete redesign while maintaining its core mission of accessibility suggests a healthy development ecosystem with sufficient community support and resources to invest in major updates.

title: Alienware’s refurbished 16 Aurora is almost $200 off at Woot
summary: Gaming laptop deals aren’t what they used to be (stares daggers at RAMageddon), which is why I consider Woot’s deal on a refurbished Alienware 16 Aurora gaming laptop with Nvidia’s RTX 5050 a pretty good deal at $927 for new Woot customers (with code WOOTALIEN used at checkout).…
whatHappening: Woot is offering a refurbished Alienware 16 Aurora gaming laptop with an Nvidia RTX 5050 GPU at a significant discount, priced at $927 for new customers using a promotional code. The deal represents nearly $200 off the regular price in a gaming laptop market where discounts have become increasingly rare.
whoInvolved: Alienware, an American gaming computer brand owned by Dell Inc. since its founding in 1996, is the manufacturer of the Aurora laptop being discounted. Woot, an Amazon-owned marketplace, is running the promotional sale and offering the refurbished unit to deal-seeking customers.
whyMatters: As gaming laptop deals have dried up in recent months, this offer provides an accessible entry point for gamers seeking high-performance hardware at a lower price. The availability of refurbished units at steep discounts also reflects shifting consumer interest in cost-effective alternatives to full-price new purchases.
articleBody:
Woot, the Amazon-owned deal marketplace, is offering a substantial discount on Alienware's 16 Aurora gaming laptop, with prices starting at $927 for new customers who apply the code WOOTALIEN at checkout. The refurbished model comes equipped with Nvidia's RTX 5050 graphics processor, a professional visual computing platform that serves both mainstream gaming and professional workstation applications in fields ranging from architecture and product design to scientific visualization and film production.

Alienware Corporation, a Miami-based subsidiary of Dell Inc., has built its reputation since 1996 on gaming-focused hardware distinguished by its alien-themed designs. The Aurora line represents the company's commitment to delivering performance-oriented machines for the gaming market. The RTX 5050 GPU included in this configuration brings substantial graphical capability to the system, making it suitable for demanding games and creative workloads alike.

According to The Verge, this deal marks a notable opportunity in a market where gaming laptop discounts have become increasingly sparse. The gaming laptop category has seen fewer aggressive price reductions recently, making promotional offerings of this magnitude noteworthy for budget-conscious buyers. The $200 savings on a refurbished unit provides meaningful value compared to typical retail pricing.

Refurbished devices occupy an important segment in the consumer electronics market, offering certified second-hand or lightly used equipment at substantially reduced prices compared to new inventory. For laptop buyers, refurbished models can deliver the same core performance and capabilities as new units while significantly lowering the barrier to entry for high-end gaming hardware. Woot's promotion specifically targets new customers, using the promotional code as a gateway to attract first-time buyers to the platform.

The timing of this promotion underscores broader consumer behavior patterns in the PC gaming space, where refurbished and discounted inventory plays an increasingly important role in hardware accessibility. Gaming laptops with dedicated graphics processors like the RTX 5050 typically command premium prices when sold new, making discounted refurbished options particularly attractive to price-sensitive buyers seeking powerful machines without the full retail expense.

title: Lexar’s Muse is an ultra-slim portable SSD that’s less than 4mm thick
summary: Following the lead of companies like Xteink, Lexar is the latest to sacrifice a USB-C port in the pursuit of slimming down its hardware. When the Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD launches later this year in 512GB and 1TB capacities it will be one of the slimmest you can buy.…
whatHappening: Lexar is launching an ultra-slim portable SSD called the Muse that measures less than 4mm thick, joining competitors in eliminating the USB-C port to achieve an exceptionally thin profile. The drive will be available later this year in 512GB and 1TB capacities.
whoInvolved: Lexar International is an American flash memory company based in San Jose that has specialized in memory product design for years; since 2017 it has operated as a subsidiary of Longsys, a Chinese flash memory manufacturer. Competitors like Xteink are also pursuing similar ultra-slim designs.
whyMatters: The trend toward sacrificing conventional ports for slimmer hardware marks a shift in how manufacturers prioritize portability and design aesthetics in storage devices. As SSDs become thinner and more competitive, consumers gain access to more compact options, though the removal of standard USB-C ports may create friction in daily use and charging workflows.
articleBody:
Lexar is pushing the boundaries of portable storage design with its upcoming Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD, a drive engineered to measure less than 4mm in thickness—making it one of the slimmest options available when it launches later this year. The company is achieving this remarkable thinness by eliminating the USB-C port entirely, a design choice that puts it in step with competitors like Xteink who have made similar trade-offs in pursuit of form-factor minimalism.

Lexar International, based in San Jose, California, has built its reputation over decades as a specialist in flash memory product design. The company, now a subsidiary of Longsys—a Shenzhen-based flash memory manufacturer that acquired it in 2017—continues to innovate in the portable storage segment. The Muse represents the company's latest entry into an increasingly competitive category where thin and light have become key selling points.

The drive will launch in two capacities: 512GB and 1TB, offering consumers familiar storage options in an unprecedented form factor. According to The Verge, the ultra-slim profile comes at the cost of traditional connectivity, which may require buyers to rely on adapters or alternative connection methods. This design philosophy reflects a broader debate in consumer electronics between maximum portability and ease of use.

The move toward port-free or port-minimal designs in storage devices illustrates how manufacturers are willing to challenge conventional expectations to differentiate their products. Whether consumers will embrace a drive that sacrifices standard USB-C connectivity for a thinner chassis remains to be seen, but the market's appetite for increasingly compact technology suggests there is genuine demand for such innovations.

title: Aqara goes all in on smart lighting
summary: After showing off several smart home firsts at CES, Aqara has returned to IFA with a major lineup of smart lighting compatible with both Zigbee and Thread. One of these new devices is the Floor Lamp T1, which trades the look of a typical lamp for an LED-equipped pole attached to…
whatHappening: Aqara is expanding its smart home ambitions with a comprehensive new lighting lineup unveiled at IFA. The company's offerings now support both Zigbee and Thread connectivity, including a redesigned Floor Lamp T1 that replaces traditional lampshade aesthetics with an LED-equipped pole design.
whoInvolved: Aqara is a smart home device manufacturer that has been building momentum in the connected home space, having recently showcased several smart home innovations at CES. The company is positioning itself as a competitor in the increasingly crowded smart lighting market dominated by larger players.
whyMatters: This move signals Aqara's commitment to establishing itself as a full-spectrum smart home platform rather than a single-category player. By supporting both major wireless protocols—Zigbee and Thread—Aqara is hedging its bets on competing standards and making its ecosystem more accessible to consumers with different smart home setups, potentially accelerating adoption among users who have already invested in either protocol.
articleBody:
Aqara has unveiled an ambitious new smart lighting portfolio at IFA, demonstrating the company's intent to become a major player in the connected home market beyond its current product focus. According to The Verge, the company is returning to the annual Berlin tech conference with a major lineup of smart lighting products designed to work with both Zigbee and Thread—two competing wireless standards that have divided the smart home industry. This dual-protocol approach represents a strategic decision to avoid being locked into a single technology ecosystem.

Among the new products is the Floor Lamp T1, a departure from conventional lamp design that replaces a traditional lampshade with an LED-equipped pole. This design choice suggests Aqara is willing to rethink fundamental product form factors rather than simply digitizing existing hardware. The device exemplifies how smart home companies are using connectivity as an opportunity to reimagine everyday objects, not merely add control features to existing designs.

The announcement builds on momentum Aqara generated at CES earlier this year, where the company showcased several smart home firsts that caught industry attention. The company's strategy of attending major consumer electronics shows demonstrates its ambitions to compete at a global scale. By revealing new capabilities at consecutive major events, Aqara is maintaining visibility in a market where consumer awareness remains fragmented.

The decision to support both Zigbee and Thread reflects broader uncertainty in the smart home industry about which wireless standard will ultimately dominate. Zigbee has long been established in the smart home space, while Thread represents a newer alternative backed by major tech companies. For consumers, this fragmentation has been frustrating—a product supporting only one protocol could become obsolete if the market consolidates around the other. Aqara's dual-support approach reduces this risk for buyers.

Smart lighting represents a logical expansion category for Aqara, given how central it is to most smart home installations. Lighting is often one of the first systems consumers automate, making it a high-volume market segment. By offering a complete ecosystem of lighting products with compatible protocols, Aqara can serve as a one-stop shop for consumers building out their connected homes.

title: You can watch the coolant flow inside Ugreen’s liquid-cooled power bank
summary: Does your power bank have "CryoPulse technology" or a "Cyber Window"? If you disappointingly answered "no" to both, you might want to consider upgrading to Ugreen's new MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank. It's available starting today for $149.99, which puts it on the really…
whatHappening: Ugreen has launched the MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank, a liquid-cooled portable charger featuring a transparent window that lets users watch coolant circulate through the device. The premium accessory is priced at $149.99 and available starting today.
whoInvolved: Ugreen is a Chinese consumer electronics brand based in Shenzhen that specializes in USB hardware, wireless chargers, and mobile accessories. Founded in 2012 by Zhang Qingsen, the company has expanded into various consumer tech categories and is now venturing into high-end power bank design.
whyMatters: The move signals how manufacturers are blending aesthetic appeal with functional cooling technology in portable electronics, targeting consumers willing to pay premium prices for visually distinctive products. As power banks become more powerful and compact, thermal management becomes increasingly important, and Ugreen's approach demonstrates one way brands can address both performance and consumer desire for premium design.
articleBody:
Ugreen has entered the premium power bank market with an unconventional approach: making the cooling system itself part of the appeal. The company's new MagFlow Pro Magnetic Power Bank, available today for $149.99, features what Ugreen calls "CryoPulse technology" and a "Cyber Window" that allows users to see the coolant actively flowing through the device during use. The transparent design transforms a typically hidden internal component into a visual feature.

The MagFlow Pro represents Ugreen's push into more sophisticated product categories. The Shenzhen-based company, established in 2012 by Zhang Qingsen, has built its reputation on USB hardware like cables and adapters, but has gradually expanded into wireless chargers, audio equipment, and other mobile accessories. This liquid-cooled power bank signals ambitions to compete at the higher end of the portable charging market, where aesthetics and premium features command higher prices.

Liquid cooling in consumer electronics is not entirely new, but its integration into portable power banks remains relatively uncommon. The technology is designed to manage heat more effectively than traditional air cooling, particularly important as power banks deliver higher wattages to charge multiple devices or larger batteries simultaneously. By making the cooling visible through a transparent window, Ugreen transforms what is functionally a heat-management solution into a product differentiator that appeals to consumers interested in the technical specs and visual design of their gadgets.

According to The Verge, the $149.99 price point positions the MagFlow Pro in the premium accessory category, where buyers expect distinctive design elements alongside core functionality. This pricing strategy reflects a broader shift in the portable charger market, where consumers increasingly view power banks as lifestyle products rather than purely utilitarian devices. Magnetic attachment compatibility suggests the device is optimized for iPhone integration, aligning with the current trend of magnetic accessories in the Apple ecosystem.

The launch underscores how thermal management and visual design are converging in consumer electronics. As batteries become denser and charging speeds increase, managing heat without compromising portability becomes a central engineering challenge. Ugreen's decision to showcase rather than conceal this solution suggests confidence that consumers value both the performance benefits and the distinctive appearance such technology provides.

title: Google says its AI weather model is getting better
summary: Google is rolling out an updated AI weather model that's supposed to be more accurate, especially when it comes to predicting rain and snowfall. In the announcement today, the company says it's now able to make forecasts with "unprecedented resolution" using its new WeatherNext…
whatHappening: Google is launching an updated AI weather model designed to deliver more accurate forecasts with greater precision, particularly for predicting rain and snowfall. The company claims its new WeatherNext system can generate predictions with unprecedented resolution.
whoInvolved: Google LLC, the American multinational technology corporation, is behind the development. Google is a major player in AI and cloud computing, with its parent company Alphabet Inc. recognized as one of the world's most valuable brands and a leading Big Tech firm.
whyMatters: More accurate weather forecasting could improve emergency preparedness, agricultural planning, and everyday decision-making for billions of users. As AI weather models become more precise, they demonstrate the expanding real-world applications of machine learning and could influence how weather services operate globally.
articleBody:
Google is rolling out a significantly improved artificial intelligence weather model that promises greater accuracy in forecasting, with particular emphasis on predicting precipitation events like rain and snowfall. According to The Verge, the company announced today that its new WeatherNext system is capable of generating forecasts with what Google describes as unprecedented resolution.

The advancement represents a meaningful step forward in computational meteorology. Traditional weather forecasting relies on complex physics-based models that simulate atmospheric conditions, but machine learning approaches can identify patterns in historical data that sometimes elude conventional methods. Google's investment in this technology underscores the company's broader expansion into artificial intelligence across its product portfolio. As an American multinational corporation with significant resources devoted to AI research and cloud computing infrastructure, Google is well-positioned to develop and deploy sophisticated weather prediction systems at scale.

Precipitation forecasting has long been one of the most challenging aspects of weather prediction. Rain and snow events are inherently variable and localized, making them difficult to predict with high confidence using traditional models. A system that improves accuracy in these specific categories could prove particularly valuable for applications ranging from urban infrastructure planning to agricultural operations to aviation safety.

The timing of this announcement reflects the broader industry trend toward machine learning applications in traditionally physics-based domains. Weather forecasting generates enormous amounts of historical data—temperature, pressure, wind speed, humidity, and countless other variables—that AI systems can analyze to improve prediction accuracy. Google's development of WeatherNext suggests the company believes AI-driven approaches can add meaningful value even in a field where meteorologists have spent decades refining computational models.

The rollout of this updated model will likely reach users through Google's existing platforms, including its search engine and weather services. The company's reach and infrastructure mean that improvements to its forecasting capability could affect how millions of people access weather information daily.

title: Belkin’s first trackers come ready to attach to your gear.
summary: Belkin’s SureFind Loop Cable Tag tracker includes a removable USB-C charging cable. | Image: Belkin After selling accessories for attaching Apple's AirTags to everything from keys to backpacks, Belkin is introducing its own trackers that work with either Apple's Find My or…
whatHappening: Belkin is launching its own line of tracking devices to compete in the item-finder market. The SureFind Loop Cable Tag includes a removable USB-C charging cable and works with both Apple's Find My network and other tracking systems.
whoInvolved: Belkin International, an El Segundo-based consumer electronics company known for mobile accessories, chargers, and connectivity peripherals, is entering the tracker market after years of selling third-party attachment solutions for Apple's AirTags. Apple's AirTag, a Bluetooth-based tracking device launched earlier, uses a crowdsourced Find My network of approximately one billion devices worldwide to help locate lost items.
whyMatters: Belkin's move signals growing competition in the tracker market beyond Apple's dominance, offering consumers more options with integrated features like built-in charging cables. This diversification could reshape how people choose tracking solutions, particularly for users who prefer alternatives to Apple's ecosystem or want multi-platform compatibility.
articleBody:
Belkin is entering the tracker market with its own line of tracking devices, moving beyond its established role as an accessory maker for Apple's ecosystem. The company's SureFind Loop Cable Tag represents a shift in strategy, combining tracking functionality with practical hardware—specifically, a removable USB-C charging cable that addresses a real user pain point. According to The Verge, the tracker works with either Apple's Find My or other competing platforms, giving users flexibility in which ecosystem they adopt.

For years, Belkin has built its reputation on producing mobile and computer connectivity devices, wireless chargers, power banks, charging cables, and various protective accessories for consumer and commercial use. The company capitalized on Apple's AirTag launch by creating attachment solutions—cases, loops, and mounts—that let users clip or secure the small tracking devices to keys, backpacks, and other gear. This accessory business proved lucrative as AirTags became ubiquitous, but it also positioned Belkin as dependent on Apple's product roadmap and design choices.

Now Belkin is betting on its own tracker hardware. The SureFind Loop Cable Tag's integrated USB-C cable is a notable design choice that differentiates it from competitors and speaks to a practical frustration: users often lose or forget to carry dedicated chargers. By bundling this functionality directly into the tracker's attachment mechanism, Belkin is targeting people who want a multi-use accessory rather than a single-purpose device.

The decision to make the tracker compatible with multiple platforms—both Apple's Find My network and other systems—also reflects a broader market reality. Apple's Find My network consists of approximately one billion devices worldwide that detect and anonymously report Bluetooth signals from AirTags and compatible devices. However, not all users are locked into Apple's ecosystem, and those on Android or other platforms have fewer native tracking options. By supporting multiple platforms, Belkin can reach a wider customer base than companies building exclusively around AirTag.

Belkin's entry into the tracker market comes at a time when the category has matured beyond Apple's initial offering. Other companies have also launched tracking devices, creating a competitive field where differentiation matters. For Belkin, leveraging its expertise in hardware design and power delivery—areas where it already produces chargers and cables—gives it credibility and a natural competitive advantage in creating trackers with practical add-on features.

The move also reflects changing consumer behavior around tracking technology. What started as a niche solution for finding lost keys has become mainstream, with users wanting to track everything from luggage to vehicles. Belkin's pivot from pure accessory maker to hardware manufacturer in this space positions the company to capture more value from this trend while reducing its reliance on Apple's product cycles.

title: Belkin introduces its first longer-lasting semi-solid-state power banks
summary: Belkin is joining companies like BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens with the launch of its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology. The company claims the new accessories have been "engineered to last up to 3x longer than other power banks" with the addition of a…
whatHappening: Belkin has launched its first power banks using semi-solid-state battery technology, joining a small but growing group of manufacturers adopting this intermediate battery approach. The company claims its new accessories will last up to three times longer than conventional power banks.
whoInvolved: Belkin International, Inc., an American consumer electronics company headquartered in El Segundo, California, is entering a market segment already occupied by competitors BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens. Belkin specializes in mobile and computer connectivity devices including wireless chargers, power banks, and charging cables for both consumer and commercial markets.
whyMatters: Semi-solid-state battery technology represents a meaningful step forward in power bank longevity and durability, addressing a key consumer pain point in portable charging devices. As battery technology evolves from liquid-electrolyte lithium-ion toward all-solid-state solutions, Belkin's entry signals that this intermediate approach is moving from niche to mainstream consumer products.
articleBody:
Belkin is introducing its first power banks featuring semi-solid-state battery technology, a move that positions the company alongside competitors BMX, Kuxiu, and Zens in adopting this emerging battery architecture. According to The Verge, the new accessories have been engineered to last up to three times longer than conventional power banks, addressing a persistent limitation of portable charging devices.

Semi-solid-state batteries represent an intermediate technology between traditional lithium-ion batteries with liquid electrolytes and the next-generation all-solid-state batteries that use fully solid electrolytes. This hybrid approach combines elements of both solid and liquid electrolyte systems, offering a practical balance between performance improvements and manufacturing feasibility. For power banks specifically, the extended lifespan addresses a common frustration: conventional units degrade significantly after a few years of regular charging cycles.

Belkin International has built its reputation on consumer electronics peripherals and connectivity devices. Beyond power banks, the company produces wireless chargers, charging cables, data cables, audio and video adapters, headphones, screen protectors, cases, surge protectors, docking stations, and data hubs for both consumer and commercial applications. The introduction of semi-solid-state power banks expands its portfolio in the growing category of premium portable charging solutions.

The shift toward semi-solid-state battery technology in consumer devices reflects broader industry momentum. While all-solid-state batteries have long been heralded as the future of energy storage, their manufacturing complexity and cost have delayed mainstream adoption. Semi-solid-state variants offer an achievable middle ground, with manufacturers now confident enough in the technology to bring it to consumer markets. The fact that multiple companies are simultaneously launching semi-solid-state power banks suggests the technology has reached a inflection point in commercial viability.

For consumers, the claimed threefold improvement in longevity translates to fewer replacement cycles over time, potentially offsetting any premium pricing these products may command. The extended lifespan also carries environmental implications, reducing e-waste from discarded power banks. As Belkin and competitors refine semi-solid-state implementations and scale production, prices are likely to become more competitive with conventional options.

title: Uber beats Waymo as first to launch robotaxis in London
summary: Uber beat out Waymo in launching a commercial robotaxi service in London, the city's first. The vehicles use autonomous driving tech developed by Wayve, a UK-based startup, and will initially feature safety drivers behind the wheel. The launch is a milestone for Uber, which has…
whatHappening: Uber has launched the first commercial robotaxi service in London, beating Waymo to market. The vehicles are powered by autonomous driving technology developed by Wayve, a UK-based startup, and will initially operate with safety drivers on board.
whoInvolved: Uber, the ride-hailing giant, partnered with Wayve Technologies Ltd, a London-headquartered autonomous driving startup founded in 2017 by University of Cambridge researchers. Waymo, Alphabet's autonomous vehicle subsidiary, had been expected to launch in London first but was beaten to the milestone by Uber.
whyMatters: This marks a significant milestone for Uber's autonomous vehicle ambitions and validates Wayve's alternative approach to self-driving technology. The London launch represents a major step toward mainstream robotaxi adoption in the UK and demonstrates that non-US companies and approaches can compete with established players like Waymo, which already operates services across 10 US metropolitan areas.
articleBody:
Uber has achieved a major milestone by launching London's first commercial robotaxi service, outpacing Waymo in the race to bring autonomous vehicles to the British capital. The vehicles rely on autonomous driving technology developed by Wayve, a Cambridge-based startup that has taken a distinctive approach to self-driving systems using end-to-end deep learning rather than detailed 3D maps and hand-coded rules.

Wayve, founded in 2017 by researchers from the University of Cambridge, has garnered significant attention and funding for its visually-based method of teaching vehicles to drive themselves. The company's "AI driver" learns from camera data and real-world driving experience, allowing it to adapt to new environments without requiring the extensive pre-mapped infrastructure that traditional autonomous systems demand. This approach has set Wayve apart in a competitive field dominated by established players with vastly larger resources.

According to The Verge, the initial London rollout will feature safety drivers behind the wheel, a common practice during the early deployment phases of robotaxi services. This staged approach allows Uber and Wayve to gather operational data and build public confidence in the technology before moving toward fully driverless operations. The launch represents validation of Wayve's technology on a commercial scale and signals growing competition in the autonomous vehicle market beyond the United States.

Waymo, Alphabet's autonomous vehicle subsidiary, had been widely expected to lead in launching a London robotaxi service. Waymo operates public commercial robotaxi services in 10 US metropolitan areas and has demonstrated substantial scale, with 3,871 robotaxis in service and 500,000 paid rides per week as of mid-2026. However, Uber's partnership with Wayve has allowed the ride-hailing company to move quickly and leverage localized expertise.

The London launch underscores the growing maturity of autonomous vehicle technology and the emergence of alternative technical approaches beyond the dominant paradigm. Rather than competing solely on computing power and mapping resources, Wayve's learning-based model offers a pathway for faster adaptation to new cities and regulatory environments. For Uber, the service provides an opportunity to integrate autonomous vehicles into its existing ride-hailing operations and gather evidence of profitability and customer acceptance in a major global market.

title: Belkin’s kid-friendly wireless headphones are 25 percent off
summary: The SoundForm Mini 2 come in a variety of colors, and include a carrying case if you’re willing to spend a bit more. | Image: The Verge Verge readers can get a discount on Belkin’s SoundForm Mini 2 wireless headphones. The kid-focused on-ear headphones feature an 85-decibel…
whatHappening: Belkin is offering a 25 percent discount on its SoundForm Mini 2 wireless headphones, a kid-friendly model available in multiple colors with optional carrying case. The deal is available to The Verge readers.
whoInvolved: Belkin International, Inc., an American consumer electronics company headquartered in El Segundo, California, manufactures audio products including headphones and earbuds for consumer use. The Verge is reporting on the promotional offer.
whyMatters: The discount makes kid-focused audio technology more accessible to parents seeking safe listening options for children. The 85-decibel volume limit built into the SoundForm Mini 2 addresses growing parental concerns about hearing protection for young users.
articleBody:
Belkin is bringing down the price of its SoundForm Mini 2 wireless headphones by 25 percent, offering consumers a discounted entry point into the company's child-oriented audio lineup. The promotion targets parents looking for reliable, safe listening devices for their kids, with the headphones available in a variety of colors to appeal to younger users.

Belkin International has built its reputation as a consumer electronics manufacturer focused on connectivity and audio peripherals. The company, headquartered in El Segundo, California, produces a broad range of products including wireless chargers, power banks, audio and video adapters, headphones, earbuds, and protective cases. The SoundForm Mini 2 fits within Belkin's established strategy of serving both general consumer and specialized market segments.

The timing of this discount reflects ongoing market interest in pediatric audio solutions. As parents become increasingly aware of hearing health concerns and the amount of time children spend with audio devices, demand for volume-limited headphones has grown. Belkin's multi-color options and portable carrying case suggest the company is positioning the SoundForm Mini 2 as both a practical tool and an appealing consumer product for younger users.

The 25 percent reduction brings the headphones to a more competitive price point while maintaining the safety features parents seek. For The Verge readers, the promotion represents a limited-time opportunity to purchase audio equipment specifically engineered with children's needs in mind.

title: Google needs Hollywood more than the studios need AI
summary: Google has reportedly been reaching out to a number of Hollywood's biggest studios, hoping to strike licensing agreements that would allow it to train its AI models on copyrighted material in exchange for massive piles of cash. In theory, these deals would be a win-win: a huge…
whatHappening: Google is actively negotiating licensing deals with major Hollywood studios to train its AI models on copyrighted films and TV content in exchange for substantial payments. These agreements would give the tech giant legal access to proprietary creative material that has traditionally been off-limits to AI training.
whoInvolved: Google LLC, an American multinational technology corporation dominant in search, advertising, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence, is pursuing deals with Hollywood's largest film and television studios. The studios represent the entertainment industry's most valuable intellectual property creators and distributors.
whyMatters: These negotiations reveal a fundamental shift in leverage between Big Tech and traditional media—Google needs quality content to compete in generative AI, making studios valuable partners rather than competitors. The outcome will set precedent for how AI companies can access and monetize creative work, with implications for copyright law, creator compensation, and the future of AI training practices.
articleBody:
Google has begun an aggressive outreach campaign to Hollywood's biggest studios, reportedly seeking licensing agreements that would permit the company to train its artificial intelligence models on copyrighted entertainment content. In exchange, Google would provide substantial financial compensation to the studios, creating what proponents frame as a mutually beneficial arrangement. According to The Verge, these discussions represent a deliberate strategy by Google to secure high-quality training material for its AI systems.

The move signals a notable shift in the traditional power dynamics between Silicon Valley and Hollywood. Google LLC, described by the BBC as the most powerful company in the world and one of the world's most valuable brands, has historically operated with minimal constraints on data acquisition. Yet the company now finds itself in a position where it must negotiate directly with content creators rather than simply scraping or using material without permission. This reflects the legal and reputational risks surrounding unlicensed AI training on copyrighted works, as well as the competitive pressure to build models trained on premium creative material.

For Hollywood studios, the pitch represents a rare opportunity to monetize their archives at a moment when their traditional business models face disruption. Rather than allowing their content to be used for AI training without compensation—or fighting costly legal battles to prevent it—studios can negotiate upfront payments. The cash injection comes at a time when streaming services have pressured theatrical revenues and production budgets remain constrained. Yet studios must also weigh whether licensing their content for AI training could cannibalize their own creative workforce or undermine the scarcity value of their intellectual property.

The outcome of these negotiations will likely establish precedent for how generative AI companies can access copyrighted material going forward. If Google successfully secures broad licensing agreements, other tech firms will face pressure to follow suit, potentially creating a new revenue stream for content creators. Conversely, if studios refuse or demand prohibitively expensive terms, it could accelerate alternative approaches—from synthetic content generation to the development of AI models trained exclusively on licensed or public domain material.

These discussions also occur against a backdrop of ongoing legal uncertainty. Numerous lawsuits have challenged whether AI training on copyrighted material constitutes fair use or copyright infringement, with courts yet to issue definitive rulings. By negotiating proactively, Google may be attempting to establish legitimacy and reduce legal exposure while demonstrating to regulators that Big Tech can work cooperatively with content creators. For Hollywood, accepting such deals could undermine arguments in ongoing litigation that AI training harms copyright holders.

articleBody:

articleBody:

The 4K resolution combined with 120Hz refresh rate support positions the device squarely at high-performance users who value smooth motion and detailed imagery.

Brightness has historically been a limitation of projectors compared to traditional televisions, making them challenging for well-lit rooms or daytime viewing. The Iris Ultra Max's dual-iris system addresses this by dynamically controlling light output to optimize both brightness and contrast simultaneously. The all-in-one design—integrating processing, audio, and display technology into a single unit—simplifies installation compared to traditional projector setups that require separate external components.

JMGO's expansion into international distribution suggests growing confidence in the premium projector market outside Asia. As home entertainment continues to shift toward larger screens and cinema-like experiences, manufacturers are investing heavily in brightness, contrast, and processing power to compete with television technology. title: FTC lawsuit alleges Amazon has been ‘secretly and systematically’ overcharging for ads
summary: The FTC and 22 state attorneys general are suing Amazon for allegedly using a "secret ad surcharge" to drive up prices for ads on its website and app. FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson claims in a blog post on the lawsuit that the higher advertising prices "were largely passed on to…
whatHappening: The FTC and 22 state attorneys general have filed a lawsuit against Amazon, alleging the company has been systematically overcharging advertisers through a hidden fee structure. The lawsuit claims Amazon used what amounts to a "secret ad surcharge" to artificially inflate advertising prices on its platform.
whoInvolved: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC), an independent agency of the U.S. government whose principal mission is the enforcement of civil antitrust law and consumer protection, is leading the charge alongside 22 state attorneys general. Amazon, an American multinational technology and retail company, is the defendant being sued for its advertising practices.
whyMatters: If the allegations are substantiated, this case could reshape how major tech platforms price advertising services and set new precedents for FTC enforcement against dominant digital marketplaces. The lawsuit directly targets Amazon's business model in a high-growth segment and may signal more aggressive regulatory scrutiny of big tech's pricing practices going forward.
articleBody:
Federal regulators are mounting a significant legal challenge to Amazon's advertising business, alleging that the company has engaged in systematic and undisclosed price manipulation. The FTC and 22 state attorneys general filed the lawsuit claiming Amazon imposed what amounted to a secret surcharge on advertisers using its platform, driving up the overall cost of digital advertising on Amazon's website and mobile app.

According to The Verge, FTC chairman Andrew Ferguson outlined the complaint in a blog post, stating that the artificially higher advertising prices "were largely passed on to" Amazon's retail customers. The allegation is that Amazon has operated this pricing scheme deliberately and without transparent disclosure to advertisers, effectively hiding the true cost structure behind what appeared to be standard ad rates.

The Federal Trade Commission, headquartered in the Federal Trade Commission Building in Washington, D.C., shares jurisdiction over federal civil antitrust law enforcement with the Antitrust Division of the U.S. Department of Justice. This lawsuit reflects the FTC's expanding focus on how dominant platforms leverage their market position to extract value from advertisers and, indirectly, from consumers who bear the cost through higher product prices.

Amazon's advertising business has become one of the company's most profitable segments in recent years, generating tens of billions of dollars annually. The alleged surcharge scheme would have allowed Amazon to increase margins on this business while maintaining the appearance of competitive pricing. The involvement of 22 state attorneys general alongside the federal regulator underscores the broad coalition of concern about Amazon's practices.

The lawsuit represents an escalation in regulatory pressure on Amazon, which has faced multiple antitrust investigations and complaints in recent years. If successful, the FTC's case could force Amazon to restructure how it charges for advertising services and potentially impose penalties for past conduct. The outcome may also influence how other major technology platforms structure their own advertising pricing and disclosure practices.

title: New York governor to 3D-printed gun leader: ‘tell Cody I will get ahead of him’
summary: Cody Wilson, the creator of the first 3D-printed gun, announced a tool last week aimed at skirting a New York law that prevents 3D printers from making firearms - and taunting governor Kathy Hochul in the process. But Hochul isn't having it. In this week's episode of Decoder,…
whatHappening: Cody Wilson, creator of the first 3D-printed gun, has announced a new tool designed to circumvent New York's restrictions on 3D-printed firearms—and deliberately taunted Governor Kathy Hochul in the process. Hochul has fired back, vowing to outmaneuver him.
whoInvolved: Cody Wilson is an American gun rights activist and crypto-anarchist who founded Defense Distributed, a non-profit that develops and publishes open-source gun designs. Governor Kathy Hochul, New York's first female governor since 2021, has positioned herself as an opponent of gun proliferation and 3D-printing technology.
whyMatters: This escalating clash highlights the ongoing tension between digital manufacturing technology and gun regulation in America. The conflict illustrates how determined activists can use open-source design and online distribution to challenge state-level firearms laws, while also demonstrating political willingness to confront such efforts directly.
articleBody:
Cody Wilson, the gun rights activist behind Defense Distributed, has thrust himself back into the national spotlight with an announcement that directly challenges New York State's efforts to restrict 3D-printed firearms. Wilson published details of a new tool last week that he claims can help circumvent a New York law preventing 3D printers from manufacturing guns. In a pointed move, he accompanied the announcement with a taunt directed at Governor Kathy Hochul, seemingly daring her to respond.

Hochul accepted the challenge. Rather than letting the provocation pass, the New York governor issued a direct counter-message, declaring that she would move to get ahead of Wilson and his efforts. The exchange represents a rare moment of open, name-called confrontation between a state executive and a digital-age activist over the future of firearms manufacturing.

Wilson has a long track record with this issue. In 2013, his organization Defense Distributed gained international attention when it published online plans for the Liberator, the first widely available functioning 3D-printed pistol. That release sparked years of legal battles and public debate over whether open-source gun designs constitute protected speech or dangerous weapons manufacturing. According to The Verge, Wilson's latest move appears designed to test the boundaries of New York's newer safeguards against 3D-printed gun production.

Hochul's response signals that New York State intends to remain aggressive in defending its regulations. As the first female governor of New York and a Democrat, Hochul has positioned herself prominently on gun control issues. Her public commitment to "get ahead of" Wilson suggests she may be considering additional legislative or enforcement measures to close loopholes or accelerate regulation of the tools and techniques Wilson is promoting.

The standoff reflects a fundamental clash between technological accessibility and governmental authority. Wilson's crypto-anarchist philosophy emphasizes the democratization of manufacturing—the idea that digital designs and open-source sharing undermine centralized control. Hochul's position represents the opposing view: that government has both the right and responsibility to restrict dangerous technologies, particularly when they circumvent existing weapons laws.

What remains unclear is whether this public sparring will lead to concrete new legislation, enforcement actions, or simply remain a battle of rhetoric and competing visions for the future of manufacturing and individual liberty.

title: Enormous 12TB Steam leak includes abandoned Half-Life 2: Episode 3 assets
summary: Over 12 terabytes of data, containing builds of every game uploaded to Steam between 2003 and 2013, has been leaked. We don't know everything in the archives yet because of its massive size. But people have already dug up assets related to the canceled Half-Life 2: Episode 3,…
whatHappening: A massive 12-terabyte data leak has exposed builds of every game uploaded to Steam between 2003 and 2013, including assets from the long-canceled Half-Life 2: Episode 3. Researchers are still cataloging the archive's full contents due to its enormous size, but abandoned development materials are already surfacing.
whoInvolved: Valve Corporation, the American video game developer and publisher headquartered in Bellevue, Washington, is the primary company affected. Valve owns Steam, the digital distribution service that hosted these game builds, and developed the Half-Life franchise, which has been dormant for nearly two decades.
whyMatters: The leak exposes sensitive development data spanning a critical decade in gaming history and reveals what might have been in a long-awaited sequel that fans have speculated about for years. It raises security concerns about the integrity of historical game archives and could affect how studios handle legacy code and unreleased assets going forward.
articleBody:
Over 12 terabytes of Steam data spanning a decade of game development has leaked online, offering an unprecedented window into the evolution of digital gaming from 2003 to 2013. The archive contains builds of every game uploaded to Steam during that period, making it one of the largest gaming leaks in history. According to The Verge, the sheer volume of the leaked data means its full contents remain unknown, with researchers still combing through the files to catalog what was included.

Among the discoveries already made are assets related to Half-Life 2: Episode 3, the long-canceled sequel that Valve never officially released. Half-Life 2, a landmark 2004 first-person shooter that introduced physics-based gameplay and vehicle mechanics to the genre, spawned two episodic sequels after its initial release. Episode Three was announced but ultimately abandoned, leaving fans to speculate for nearly two decades about what the game might have contained. The leaked assets provide tangible evidence of the development work that went into the project before it was shelved.

Valve Corporation, which developed Half-Life and numerous other major gaming franchises including Counter-Strike, Portal, and Team Fortress, has not yet publicly commented on the breach. The company, also known as Valve Software, operates Steam as its primary digital distribution platform, which revolutionized how games reach consumers. The leaked data effectively captures Steam's earliest years and the diversity of titles published during gaming's shift toward digital delivery.

The leak raises significant questions about data security and the preservation of gaming history. Development builds and assets from unreleased games are typically confidential material that studios guard closely. The exposure of a decade's worth of such material—including abandoned projects, early iterations of released games, and potentially proprietary tools—could have implications for how companies handle archival and legacy data going forward.

For enthusiasts and historians, the leak offers rare insight into the creative process behind some of gaming's most influential titles. Researchers are expected to spend considerable time examining the archive, potentially uncovering stories about canceled games, development timelines, and design decisions that shaped the industry during a transformative period. The Half-Life 2: Episode 3 materials are just the beginning of what may prove to be a treasure trove of gaming history.

title: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches to study dark matter and dark energy
summary: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope blasts off. | Photo: NASA / John Kraus After funding struggles and a name change, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has been successfully launched. It will now make a three-month, one-million-mile journey to its orbit at the second…
whatHappening: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has successfully launched into space after years of funding challenges and delays. The observatory is now beginning a three-month journey covering one million miles to reach its operational orbit at the Sun-Earth L2 point, where it will study dark matter and dark energy.
whoInvolved: NASA developed and launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is named after Nancy Grace Roman, the first female executive at NASA who served as the agency's chief of astronomy throughout the 1960s and 1970s. The mission represents a continuation of Roman's legacy as one of the visionary founders of the U.S. civilian space program.
whyMatters: The Roman Space Telescope will conduct unprecedented observations of dark matter and dark energy, addressing some of astronomy's most fundamental questions about the composition and expansion of the universe. Success of this long-delayed mission validates NASA's commitment to large-scale observatories and provides crucial data for cosmology research for years to come.
articleBody:
After navigating significant funding obstacles and a name change, NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has officially launched on its mission to study the universe's most elusive components. The observatory is now embarking on a three-month voyage across one million miles of space to reach its destination at the second Lagrange point between the Sun and Earth, according to The Verge, where it will begin its observations of dark matter and dark energy.

The telescope carries considerable historical significance, named after Nancy Grace Roman, a pioneering astronomer who became NASA's first chief of astronomy in the 1960s and 1970s. Roman made fundamental contributions to stellar classification and stellar motions during her career, and her leadership established her as one of the visionary founders of the U.S. civilian space program. Naming the observatory after her honors both her scientific achievements and her role in shaping America's space ambitions during the agency's formative decades.

The road to launch was not straightforward. The mission faced substantial funding challenges and underwent a name change before finally reaching the launch pad. These obstacles reflected both the complexity of building a world-class space observatory and the budget pressures facing large scientific projects. Despite these hurdles, the successful launch represents a major milestone for NASA and the astronomical community.

Once Roman reaches its L2 orbit, the telescope will be positioned approximately one million miles from Earth in a gravitationally stable location that minimizes interference from the Sun and Earth's radiation. From this vantage point, it will conduct infrared observations designed to probe the nature of dark matter and dark energy, the two most mysterious components of the cosmos that together comprise roughly 95 percent of the universe's content.

The mission's focus on dark matter and dark energy addresses fundamental questions that have driven cosmological research for decades. By mapping the distribution of dark matter and measuring how dark energy influences cosmic expansion, the Roman Space Telescope will help refine our understanding of the universe's past, present, and ultimate fate. These observations will complement other major observatories and contribute crucial data for multiple fields within astronomy.

The rediscovery underscores the value of physical media archives and the role they play in preserving underground music history that might otherwise fade from collective memory.
articleBody:
Digging through old CD collections has become an increasingly common way for longtime music fans to reconnect with forgotten releases from earlier eras. One such discovery has brought renewed attention to the Professor Murder Rides the Subway EP, a concise and meticulously crafted work from the mid-2000s New York indie scene that few people seem to remember today.

The mid-2000s represented a particularly fertile period for experimental music in New York City, when the line between dance music, punk, and indie rock was deliberately blurred by a generation of artists eager to challenge genre conventions. According to The Verge, this was an era when "it seemed like every indie" act in the city was pushing boundaries and creating hybrid sounds that defied easy categorization. Professor Murder was part of this broader ecosystem, crafting a sound that combined the kinetic energy of punk with the rhythmic sophistication of electronic and dance music.

What makes the Professor Murder Rides the Subway EP notable is its conciseness and apparent lack of filler. In an era when even EPs could feel bloated or underdeveloped, this release demonstrated disciplined songwriting and production choices. The work captures a specific moment in time when the New York underground was generating significant creative energy, yet most of the acts from this period have since faded into relative obscurity.

The rediscovery of such records raises important questions about music preservation and accessibility. Physical media archives like personal CD collections have become unintended repositories of musical history, holding releases that may never have been widely available digitally or through streaming platforms. As more people digitize these collections, they create opportunities for smaller and more experimental works to resurface and be reassessed by new audiences.

Today, the dance punk movement of the mid-2000s New York scene occupies an interesting cultural position. While some acts from that era have maintained relevance or cult followings, many others have largely disappeared from mainstream conversation. The Professor Murder Rides the Subway EP exemplifies this phenomenon—a focused, well-executed work from an important time and place that somehow slipped through the cracks of music history and collective memory.

title: Chess.com launched a poker site and is planning even more classic games
summary: Chess.com has done one thing, and one thing very well, for almost 20 years, but now it's going beyond its domain name. The biggest name in online chess quietly launched its first companion site in beta back in May: Gambit, a free online poker website where players can learn the…
whatHappening: Chess.com, the world's dominant online chess platform, has quietly launched Gambit, a free poker website, signaling its expansion beyond chess into other classic games. The company is planning to add even more games to its portfolio in the coming months.
whoInvolved: Chess.com is the largest chess platform in the world, operating on a freemium model with millions of users playing live chess in various time controls, analyzing games, and learning from educational resources. The Verge reports on this strategic pivot.
whyMatters: Chess.com's diversification could reshape how players view the company—transforming it from a single-game specialist into a broader gaming platform. Success with poker and additional games could unlock new revenue streams and user bases, while risking dilution of the brand identity that made Chess.com the market leader in online chess.
articleBody:
Chess.com has spent nearly two decades establishing itself as the global standard for online chess, but the company is now venturing into unfamiliar territory. The platform quietly launched Gambit, its first companion site, in beta back in May. Gambit is a free online poker website designed to help players learn the game, marking Chess.com's first major expansion beyond the 64 squares that made it famous.

Chess.com's core offering has remained tightly focused since its inception. The site operates on a freemium model where basic features—including live online chess games against other users in daily, rapid, blitz, and bullet time controls—are available for free, while advanced features and premium analysis tools require a subscription. The platform also offers play against chess engines, computer analysis, chess puzzles, and teaching resources. This singular focus has helped Chess.com become the largest chess platform in the world, attracting millions of players worldwide.

The launch of Gambit suggests Chess.com's leadership believes there is untapped potential in parlaying its reputation and user base into adjacent gaming categories. According to The Verge, the company is planning even more classic games beyond poker, though specific titles and timelines have not been announced. The approach mirrors successful gaming platforms that have expanded from strength in one category into others.

Poker presents a natural complement to chess in some ways—both involve strategic decision-making, reading opponents, and managing probability. However, the games appeal to different skill sets and player psychologies. Poker is a family of comparing card games in which players wager over which hand is best, played worldwide with varying rules and deck configurations. The learning curve and community dynamics differ significantly from chess, meaning Chess.com will need to build distinct expertise and culture for Gambit if it hopes to compete in poker's crowded online marketplace.

The beta launch in May, if indeed quiet, suggests Chess.com is testing the waters carefully before making any major commitment. Whether Gambit and its planned successors will attract the devoted, competitive communities that Chess.com cultivated in chess remains an open question. The company's decision to remain freemium across platforms suggests a bet that user acquisition and engagement matter more than immediate monetization in emerging categories.

title: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported
summary: Alt-right troll Milo Yiannopoulos was arrested by ICE on Thursday, and today the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Reuters and the Washington Post that he had been deported to the UK. Yiannopoulos came to the US legally in 2019, but overstayed his visa. After he…
whatHappening: Milo Yiannopoulos, a prominent far-right political commentator, has been deported to the UK after being arrested by ICE. The Department of Homeland Security confirmed the deportation following his overstay of his US visa.
whoInvolved: Milo Yiannopoulos is a British far-right commentator and former editor of Breitbart News known for his opposition to Islam, feminism, and social justice. The arrest and deportation were carried out by ICE, the federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Homeland Security responsible for enforcing immigration laws and preserving national security.
whyMatters: The deportation highlights enforcement of immigration law against a high-profile political figure who had entered the country legally but overstayed his visa. It raises questions about visa compliance among public figures and demonstrates DHS's willingness to enforce immigration violations regardless of a person's prominence or media presence.
articleBody:
Milo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator and former editor of Breitbart News, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Thursday and has since been deported to the United Kingdom. According to The Verge, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed the deportation to Reuters and the Washington Post.

Yiannopoulos initially entered the United States legally in 2019 but subsequently overstayed his visa, triggering the immigration enforcement action. The circumstances leading to his arrest suggest that ICE had identified the visa violation and moved to enforce compliance through deportation proceedings.

ICE, created as part of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, operates as a federal law enforcement agency tasked with conducting criminal investigations, enforcing immigration laws, preserving national security, and protecting public safety. The agency absorbed the prior functions of the Immigration and Naturalization Service and the United States Customs Service. Yiannopoulos's deportation represents the agency's enforcement of immigration statutes against an individual who had overstayed his authorized period of residence.

Yiannopoulos is known internationally for his provocative political commentary opposing Islam, feminism, and social justice causes. His career in media and politics has made him a visible figure in far-right circles, and his removal from the United States may have implications for his platform and influence in American political discourse. The British commentator's deportation underscores that visa violations, regardless of a person's public profile or political prominence, remain subject to federal enforcement action.

The case also reflects broader patterns of immigration enforcement, where individuals who enter the country legally but fail to maintain their visa status face removal proceedings. Yiannopoulos's status as a public figure did not shield him from the standard deportation process, suggesting consistent application of immigration law across different sectors of society.

title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic
summary: Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for "tens of thousands" copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance…
whatHappening: Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed a lawsuit against Anthropic in federal court, alleging the AI company used tens of thousands of copyrighted musical works without permission to train its Claude language model. The plaintiffs are seeking damages of up to $150,000 per work, potentially reaching into the billions.
whoInvolved: Sony Music Entertainment is the recording division of Sony Group Corporation and one of the world's largest music companies. Warner Chappell is a major music publishing entity. Anthropic, PBC is a San Francisco-based AI company founded in 2021 by former OpenAI members including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, best known for developing Claude, a series of large language models.
whyMatters: This case represents a significant legal challenge to how AI companies obtain training data, potentially setting precedent for the music industry's relationship with generative AI developers. The outcome could force major changes in how AI firms source and compensate for copyrighted content, with ripple effects across the broader AI training ecosystem.
articleBody:
Sony Music and Warner Chappell have brought legal action against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, accusing the artificial intelligence company of copyright infringement on a massive scale. According to The Verge, the suit targets the use of tens of thousands of copyrighted musical works in training Anthropic's AI models, with the plaintiffs seeking damages of up to $150,000 per work and up to $25,000 for each instance of infringement.

Anthropric, the San Francisco-based AI company founded in 2021 by former OpenAI members Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, has built its reputation on Claude, a series of proprietary large language models designed to perform a wide range of tasks. Like other generative AI systems, Claude's capabilities depend on training on large datasets drawn from the internet and other sources. The question of what data can legally be used for this purpose has become increasingly contentious as the AI industry expands.

The lawsuit from Sony Music Entertainment—the recording division of Sony Group Corporation and one of the world's largest music companies—alongside Warner Chappell, one of the major music publishing entities, signals that the creative industries are prepared to pursue aggressive legal strategies against AI developers. The combination of broad infringement claims and substantial statutory damages reflects the stakes involved in this emerging area of intellectual property law.

The music industry's response to generative AI has been notably swift and forceful compared to some other sectors. Unlike some publishers or authors who have taken varied approaches to AI training, major record labels and music publishers appear unified in their view that large-scale use of their catalogs without licensing or compensation crosses a legal and ethical line. The specific damages framework—which includes both per-work penalties and per-instance charges—suggests the plaintiffs view the infringement as systematic rather than incidental.

This case arrives as Anthropic, which remains privately held, reportedly plans an initial public offering for fall 2026. A significant legal judgment or settlement could have material financial implications for the company as it prepares for public markets. More broadly, the outcome may influence how other tech companies approach data sourcing and whether existing copyright frameworks prove adequate for regulating AI training practices.

title: Vicariously hike the Appalachian in the gorgeous A Trail Tale
